finding.title: Buffer Overflow
finding.trigger: num is very large, causing sprintf to write beyond the bounds of buffer
finding.assumptions: The size of buffer is fixed at 50, and there is no check to ensure that the formatted string fits within this buffer. If num is very large, the formatted string could exceed 50 characters, leading to a buffer overflow.

parsed.refutation_attempt: Checked the maximum possible length of an int when formatted with "%d". The largest 32‑bit signed integer is 2,147,483,647, which requires 10 digits plus an optional sign, totaling at most 11 characters including the terminating null. The buffer is declared as 50 bytes, so there is ample space. No other code path can increase the size of the formatted string beyond this bound. Therefore the sprintf call cannot overflow the buffer.

finding.title: OS Command Injection
finding.trigger: formattedNum contains attacker-controlled data that could be crafted to inject malicious commands
finding.assumptions: The code does not sanitize or validate the input before using it in printf. If an attacker can control the input to format_with_commas, they could potentially inject malicious commands.

parsed.refutation_attempt: The reported source "formattedNum" is not untrusted. It is produced by format_with_commas, which takes an int argument. In main, the int is a compile‑time constant (7000000). Therefore the data cannot be controlled by an attacker. Additionally, the sink is printf("%s\n", formattedNum); which uses a fixed format string; any format specifiers in formattedNum would be printed literally, not interpreted as format directives. Thus there is no path from untrusted input to a command‑execution sink, and no command injection is possible.
